html:
The building blocks are hard-wired reflexes (e.g rooting, grasping, startle); during this stage, the infant gains control over involuntary movements. Skills in this tier consist of innate actions that require direct physical or socio-emotional stimulation for their evocation.

Fischer treats this as a corollary/starting point: the infant begins with single reflexes then coordinates them into reflex mappings, then reflex systems, then systems of reflex systems, which can yield a flexible single sensorimotor action (like robust "looking").

Level 1: Single Reflexes ( 3-4 weeks)

The infant has a single, specific reflex in response to a stimulus.

Example 1: Hold the infant upright with feet touching a surface and you see alternating step-like leg movements (the stepping reflex)

Example 2: A baby closes their hand when a finger touches their palm (the palmar grasp reflex). This is an isolated action, not yet coordinated with looking or reaching.

Example 3: A baby turns their head and opens their mouth towards a touch on the cheek to find a breast or bottle, helping them feed (the rooting reflex)

Example 4: Something touches the lips/roof of the mouth and you get rhythmic sucking (the sucking reflex)

Example 5: A sudden loud noise or movement makes the baby throw their arms out and then pull them back in, as if to embrace someone (the Moro (startle) reflex)

Level 2: Reflex Mappings ( 7-8 weeks)

The infant coordinates two distinct reflexes into a single action pattern.

Example 1: The infant hears a sound (auditory reflex) and turns their eyes toward it (visual reflex). They have "mapped" hearing to looking.

Example 2: visual swiping (Visually Elicited Reaching); the infant coordinates visual fixation with arm extension. Upon locking eyes on an interesting object (visual reflex), the infant immediately flings their arm toward it (motor reflex). This is distinct from Level 3 because it is ballistic: they "swipe" at where they see the object, but they cannot yet correct their hand’s path mid-flight if they miss.

Example 3: The Traction Response (Grasp-Pull Mapping); the infant coordinates the palmar grasp with arm flexion. When an adult’s finger touches the infant’s palm, they grasp it (reflex 1). Once the grip is secure, they automatically tense and flex their biceps (reflex 2) to pull their torso up. The two reflexes are now mapped into a single "pulling" unit.

Level 3: Reflex Systems ( 10-11 weeks)

Multiple reflex mappings are integrated into a complex, continuous feedback loop. The infant can now vary their action to maintain a specific result. This effectively generates the first Single Sensorimotor Actions (which become the single "units" of Tier 1).

Example 1: Tracking a moving object. The infant sees an object (vision), turns their head (motor), and adjusts their focus (accommodation) continuously as the object moves.

Example 2: Visually-guided reaching. This is the evolution of the "Visual Swipe" (Level 2). The infant sees the object, moves the hand, sees the hand’s position relative to the object, and corrects the trajectory mid-air. It integrates vision, proprioception, and motor control into a loop: Look→Reach→Compare→Adjust→GraspLook \rightarrow Reach \rightarrow Compare \rightarrow Adjust \rightarrow Grasp.

Example 3: Suck-Swallow-Breathe (The Feeding System). This requires the precise, rhythmic sequencing of three distinct reflexes: sucking (extracting liquid), swallowing (transporting liquid to the esophagus), and breathing (protecting the airway). Unlike a simple mapping, this is a system: if the milk flow is too fast, the infant adjusts the breathing/swallowing ratio. If they need air, they pause the sucking. The components work together dynamically.
